'''Galit Lahav''' ({{Langx|he|גלית להב}}; born 1973) is an Israeli-American [[Systems biology|systems biologist]] and Professor of Systems Biology at [[Harvard Medical School]]. In 2018 she became Chair of the Department of Systems Biology at Harvard Medical School.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web|url=https://hms.harvard.edu/news/new-systems-bio-chair-named|title=New Systems Bio Chair Named {{!}} Harvard Medical School|website=hms.harvard.edu|access-date=2019-01-26}}</ref>  She is known for discovering the pulsatile behavior of the [[tumor suppressor]] protein [[p53]]<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=Lahav|first1=Galit|last2=Rosenfeld|first2=Nitzan|last3=Sigal|first3=Alex|last4=Geva-Zatorsky|first4=Naama|last5=Levine|first5=Arnold J.|last6=Elowitz|first6=Michael B.|last7=Alon|first7=Uri|date=2004|title=Dynamics of the p53-Mdm2 feedback loop in individual cells|journal=Nature Genetics|volume=36|issue=2|pages=147–150|doi=10.1038/ng1293|issn=1061-4036|pmid=14730303|doi-access=free}}</ref> and uncovering its significance for cell fate,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://hms.harvard.edu/news/damaged-cells-feel-beat|title=Damaged Cells Feel the Beat {{!}} Harvard Medical School|website=hms.harvard.edu|access-date=2019-01-26}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last1=Lahav|first1=Galit|last2=Loewer|first2=Alexander|last3=Batchelor|first3=Eric|last4=Mock|first4=Caroline|last5=Karhohs|first5=Kyle W.|last6=Purvis|first6=Jeremy contributions to the culture of mentoring in science.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|url=https://hms.harvard.edu/news/peerless-inspiration|title=Peerless Inspiration {{!}} Harvard Medical Massachusetts.

==Education==

Lahav earned her PhD in 2001 from the [[Technion – Israel Institute of Technology|Technion]], where she studied [[transcriptional regulation]] in the laboratory of Yona Kassir. She then performed postdoctoral work in the laboratory of [[Uri Alon]] at the [[Weizmann Institute of Science]].

==Research and career==

In her postdoctoral work in the Alon lab, Lahav investigated the response of [[p53]] to DNA damage. p53 is highly studied due to its role as "guardian of the genome";<ref>{{Cite book|title=Human molecular genetics|last1=T.|first1=Strachan|date=1999|publisher=Wiley|last2=Read|first2=Andrew P.|isbn=978-0471330615|edition=2nd|location=New York|pages=Chapter 18: Cancer Genetics|oclc=41580663|url=https://archive.org/details/humanmolecularge0002stra}}</ref> in response to DNA damage, p53 activation may lead to a delay in the [[cell cycle]] to allow [[DNA repair]], or may cause the cell to undergo [[Cellular senescence|senescence]] or [[apoptosis]]. Previous work had shown that the [[feedback loop]] between p53 and its regulator [[Mdm2]] could theoretically cause oscillations in the level of p53.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last1=Lev Bar-Or|first1=Ruth|last2=Maya|first2=Ruth|last3=Segel|first3=Lee A.|last4=Alon|first4=Uri|last5=Levine|first5=Arnold J.|last6=Oren|first6=Moshe|date=2000-10-10|title=Generation of oscillations by the p53-Mdm2 feedback loop: A theoretical and experimental study |pmc=17186 |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America|volume=97|issue=21|pages=11250–11255|issn=0027-8424|pmid=11016968|doi=10.1073/pnas.210171597|bibcode=2000PNAS...9711250L |doi-access=free }}</ref> Oscillations were in fact observed in cells exposed to radiation, using a [[Western blot]] technique that measures the average p53 level in a population of cells.<ref name=":1" /> Lahav developed a novel system for following p53 levels and Mdm2 levels simultaneously in individual living cells<ref name=":0" /> and demonstrated that individual cells show discrete pulses of p53 after [[Gamma ray|gamma irradiation]]. Genetically identical cells showed different numbers of pulses: 0, 1, 2 or more.  Although the size of the pulse does not change with increasing levels of DNA damage, the average number of pulses does increase.<ref name=":0" />  In later work, Lahav showed that these pulses are not an autonomous oscillation intrinsic to the p53:Mdm2 feedback loop, but are recurrently initiated by upstream signals of continuing DNA damage.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Batchelor|first1=Eric|last2=Mock|first2=Caroline S.|last3=Bhan|first3=Irun|last4=Loewer|first4=Alexander|last5=Lahav|first5=Galit|date=2008-05-09|title=Recurrent initiation: a mechanism for triggering p53 pulses in response to DNA damage |journal=Molecular Cell |volume=30 |issue=3 |pages=277–289 |doi=10.1016/j.molcel.2008.03.016 |issn=1097-4164|pmc=2579769|pmid=18471974}}</ref> This finding suggests that p53 may measure the intensity of some signals in a digital manner (number of pulses), not in an analog manner (higher concentrations of p53).<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Arnold J. Levine|last2=Harris|first2=Sandra L.|date=2005|title=The p53 pathway: positive and negative feedback loops|journal=Oncogene|language=en|volume=24|issue=17|pages=2899–2908|doi=10.1038/sj.onc.1208615|pmid=15838523|issn=1476-5594|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Lahav then discovered that DNA damage caused by [[UV-irradiation]] results in a different p53 behavior, leading to a single pulse that increases in size and duration with increasing damage.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lahav|first1=Galit|last2=Mock|first2=Caroline|last3=Loewer|first3=Alexander|last4=Batchelor|first4=Eric|date=2011-01-01|title=Stimulus-dependent dynamics of p53 in single cells|journal=Molecular Systems Biology|language=en|volume=7|issue=1|pages=488|doi=10.1038/msb.2011.20|issn=1744-4292|pmid=21556066|pmc=3130553}}</ref> This led her to hypothesize that the dynamic behavior of p53 contained information on the nature of the damage to DNA and determined the nature of the response by the damaged cell. She developed a method for forcing a cell damaged by gamma irradiation to adopt the p53 dynamics seen in UV irradiation, based on precisely timed additions of the Mdm2 inhibitor [[Nutlin]]-3. Cells damaged using gamma irradiation without drug treatment showed cell cycle arrest and then recovered, while the same cells treated with drug to simulate UV-type p53 dynamics entered senescence and failed to divide.<ref name=":2" /> These results led Lahav to investigate whether the schedule of drug administration might affect the response to common types of [[combination therapy]] in cancer, in which drugs are given in combination with [[radiation therapy]].  She found that if radiation was given shortly after addition of an [[Mdm2]] inhibitor the treatment enhanced the effect of radiation, whereas a longer gap between the two treatments led to resistance.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lahav|first1=Galit|last2=Forrester|first2=William|last3=Chen|first3=Sheng-hong|date=2016-03-11|title=Schedule-dependent interaction between anticancer treatments|journal=Science|language=en|volume=351|issue=6278|pages=1204–1208|doi=10.1126/science.aac5610|issn=0036-8075|pmid=26965628|pmc=5217461|bibcode=2016Sci...351.1204C}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://hms.harvard.edu/news/timing-matters|title=Timing Matters |website=hms.harvard.edu|access-date=2019-01-26}}</ref> There is growing consensus that dynamics are important for signaling in multiple biological pathways.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Elowitz|first1=Michael B.|last2=Lin|first2=Yihan|last3=Levine|first3=Joe H.|date=2013-12-06|title=Functional Roles of Pulsing in Genetic Circuits|journal=Science|language=en|volume=342|issue=6163|pages=1193–1200|doi=10.1126/science.1239999|issn=0036-8075|pmid=24311681|pmc=4100686|bibcode=2013Sci...342.1193L}}</ref>

Lahav has measured the cell-to-cell variation in p53 response in colon cancer cells responding to damage by the [[chemotherapeutic]] drug [[cisplatin]]<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Paek|first1=Andrew L.|last2=Liu|first2=Julia C.|last3=Loewer|first3=Alexander|last4=Forrester|first4=William C.|last5=Lahav|first5=Galit|date=2016-04-21|title=Cell-to-Cell Variation in p53 Dynamics Leads to Fractional Killing |journal=Cell|volume=165|issue=3|pages=631–642|doi=10.1016/j.cell.2016.03.025|issn=1097-4172|pmc=5217463|pmid=27062928}}</ref> and has argued that this variation may underlie the phenomenon of [[fractional kill]], in which a fraction of cancer cells survive chemotherapeutic treatment and subsequently grow, causing a recurrence of the cancer.

Lahav joined the Department of Systems Biology at [[Harvard Medical School]] in 2004.  In 2017 she was appointed Deputy Chair, and in 2018 Dean [[George Q. Daley]] appointed her as Chair of the Department.<ref name=":5" /> In the announcement of her appointment, Daley highlighted "her pioneering role in developing computational and quantitative experimental approaches to studying the fate and behavior of human cells in disease and health at the single-cell level."<ref name=":5" />

===Contributions to mentoring===
Lahav is an advocate for improved mentoring in science. As an assistant professor, she initiated a peer-to-peer mentoring group at Harvard Medical School.<ref name=":3" /> She has written on the challenges of combining the role of a mother with the demands of a research career.<ref name=":4" /> She served as Junior Faculty Liaison for Faculty Development at Harvard Medical School from 2013 to 2018.
